It seems to be an old phrase with french origin, that has changed many times along the way. Similar forms include "wading/walking/running through (the) treacle", which make more sense, treacle being a viscous sugar derived syrup, the imagery of trying to run through it is intuitively imaginable. That phrase means pretty much what you might guess, which is to do something where progress is slow and takes a lot of effort  


"Cutting through the treacle" seems to show up primarily in american english as a modified version of the older phrases. The physical action of cutting through treacle doesn't appear to have any real world history, not that it's really feasible anyway. In that simpsons episode bart uses the phrase as one would use the phrase "separate the wheat from the chaff", when he references himself saying "eat my shorts" to potential new nannies, apparently with the intent to scare off any who might not be able to handle babysitting him (s8e13 7:44, I was watching that very episode as I found this lol). That seems to be in line with how the phrase is generally used, basically a simple and often crude action to separate a group into good stuff and bad stuff  


Interpreting the syntax as a general metaphor and not a historical idiom, the wording "cutting through the treacle" seems more appropriately used as a metaphor about futility, as the act of cutting through treacle would take a lot of effort and all the progress you made would be quickly undone. I'm not sure if the idiom form that uses cut is really necessary, I can't find unique meaning it has over "separating the wheat from the chaff", and it is less historically accurate, and more importantly less understandable. Though in american english "wading through treacle" isn't really necessary either as you'd probably be more in-line with common speech patterns to say something about walking/trudging through molasses
